files.text:
On paper

Good writing paper was once made of rags: worn linen shirts and bedsheets, left in damp heaps until they rotted soft, then beaten for hours in a trough of water until the fibres came apart, lifted on a wire mould and pressed between felts. Hold such a sheet to the light and you can still see the mould in it, fine lines close together and stronger ones an inch apart. Rag paper does not flare like newsprint. Put a corner to a flame and it smoulders. The heat runs ahead of the fire and browns the sheet as the cellulose gives up its water; then a thin edge of embers creeps forward, faster along the fibres than across them, and leaves behind a black skin of carbon that shrinks and cracks like glaze. The carbon burns more slowly still, and what is left at the end is ash, the little mineral the fibres held and the chalk the papermaker added: grey, nearly weightless, keeping the shape of the page until a breath lifts it.

Hollins Farm, 3rd October

Dear Nell,

The pears are in, the light goes by six, and the swallows left on Tuesday, all at once, the way they do. It seems the season for saying things.

When you came to help with the lambing that first spring, I learned the sound of your step on the yard stones before I learned your face. I have listened for it ever since. I never said so, because you had Tom, and then the children, and because it never asked for anything. It was only true, and I wanted one other person to know it, once.

Don't answer this. Read it at the kitchen table, put it in the range, and let us go on as we were: the eggs on Fridays, the crossword over the wall.

With my love, which is old and quiet,

Alice

Most letters of this kind were burned, as they asked to be. Cassandra Austen, late in her life, burned the greater part of her sister's letters and cut passages out of others. Dickens made a bonfire of twenty years of his correspondence in the field at Gad's Hill, and his boys roasted onions in the ashes. Others were kept against instructions, in a drawer, under the lining paper, folded in three along creases that went brown. Fire is less thorough than it looks. Iron-gall ink leaves its iron behind when the paper goes, and on the grey ash of a burned page the writing can often still be read, rust on ash, for as long as no one touches it.

# pretext-burn A handwritten letter burning slowly from one corner as you scroll, the way paper burns: the sheet browns ahead of the fire, a thin broken line of embers creeps across it, behind that the paper goes to glossy black char that cracks into plates, then to grey ash, and the ash lifts away a flake at a time and leaves holes onto the page. The words glow for a moment as the embers cross them, and the ink is still faintly there in the ash, rust on grey. Scroll back and the letter unburns through exactly the same states. Near the end the fire goes out and leaves a scorched fragment with the greeting on it. ```html

Hollins Farm, 3rd October

Dear Nell,

The pears are in …

When you came to help …

With my love, which is old and quiet,

Alice

``` Or `import { pretextBurn } from './pretext-burn.js'` and call `pretextBurn(section, options)`; it returns `destroy()`. The letter's paragraphs are read in order. Classes set their place on the sheet: `pb-date` (right-aligned), `pb-greet` (left, no indent), plain `

` (body, first line indented), `pb-close` (from a third of the way in), `pb-sign` (from just past half). 150-220 words fit well. The face is the `.pb-letter`'s own `font-family` (the demo loads Homemade Apple from Google Fonts: it reads as a real pen, and stays legible at 10px on a phone). ## Options Data attributes on the section, or the options object (which wins). | attribute | option | default | what it does | |---|---|---|---| | `data-seed` | `seed` | `11` | The paper: its thick and thin spots, fibre direction, blots of size, the plates and flakes, the hand's wobble. `random` gives a new sheet each visit. | | `data-ignite` | `ignite` | `right` | The corner the fire starts from: `right` (bottom right) or `left` (bottom left). | | `data-keep` | `keep` | `0.22` | The fraction of the sheet that never burns: the fire goes out with this much left, in the far corner. `0` burns nearly everything. | | `data-rest` | `rest` | `0.36` | With reduced motion, how far the fire has got (fraction of the whole burn) in the still frame. | | `data-aspect` | `aspect` | `1.38` | Sheet height / width (a phone may make it taller, up to 1.5). | | `data-leading` | `leading` | `1.9` | Line pitch, x the font size. | | `data-font`, `data-weight` | `font`, `weight` | the letter's | Canvas-only face, if it should differ from the fallback's. | ## How it works 1. **Writing.** pretext (Cheng Lou) prepares each paragraph once at 100px; its widths are linear in size, so a binary search re-sets the letter at eighteen trial sizes and keeps the largest that fills the sheet. Lines go out ragged, as handwriting does, with `layoutNextLine`. Each line is written onto a 2D canvas at device resolution with a hand's small irregularities: a baseline that drifts, a slight slope, words a hair off the line, and ink that is dark after each dip of the pen and runs drier over the next five to eleven words. That canvas is the ink texture. 2. **The burn-time field.** In a Worker (built from a Blob; on the main thread if a worker can't be made), a 16-neighbour Dijkstra over a grid of about 330 cells across the sheet, from the ignition corner. The local speed of burning is a product of: slow large-scale variation (thick and thin spots in the sheet), medium noise, streaks along a fibre direction (noise stretched 11:1), a few slow blots of size that the front has to go round, more air along the cut edges, a touch faster through ink. Steps along the fibres cost less (up to a quarter), and steps upward a little less (heat climbs). Each cell stores the time the fire reaches it. The fire goes out with the far fragment left (`data-keep`); any other pocket of paper the front has closed round is made faster and the field re-run until none is left inside the char. A second channel stores the front's local speed (one over the gradient), so the shader can measure distance to the front in pixels, and a third a blurred copy of the field, for the scorch. 3. **One shader thresholds it by t.** Per pixel, the distance ahead of the front in css px (plus fibre-scale noise, so the burnt edge is ragged): - ahead: the **scorch**, a heat gradient taken from the blurred field so it follows the front's broad shape rather than every finger: paper → straw → tan → brown, darkest in a narrow band against the char, mottled at fibre scale; ink in it darkens; - at the front: the **ember line**, a gaussian a couple of pixels wide, broken into beads by noise that slowly boils (two noise fields cross-faded, drifting in different directions), with dark gaps, a few hot yellow points inside the beads, a dull red tail in the char behind, and a faint orange light on the paper close by. The writing has a wider glow band than the paper, so words light up red as the line reaches them and stay lit a moment longer; - behind: **char**, near-black and satin: the sheet buckles as it chars into gentle ridges a few mm across (warped noise, loosely along the fibres), and broad soft highlights ride them. A few long splits follow the fibres in places. The leading edge rolls up off the sheet: a ridge just behind the embers whose lip catches the light, with a soft shadow on the paper ahead of it. Ink on char is a shade glossier; - **ash**, a narrow band about a third of the char's width: thin, pale silver-grey, finely wrinkled, the ink a rust ghost on it; - then it breaks into small flakes (a jittered Voronoi net, about 85 to the sheet's width), each lifting at its own moment (its centre's burn time + a jitter), cupping and showing hairline breaks just before it goes. The hole shows the page with a soft shadow from the sheet's lifted edges and a little fallen ash; its edge is antialiased against the neighbour that has lifted. 4. **Particles.** Each flake that lifts may (45%) leave as a particle: the very cell whose hole has just opened, rising on the convection, fluttering, turning over (one face paler than the other), shrinking and fading over 2.5-5 s. Smoke is soft grey sprites rising from points on the current ember line, growing and fading over 5-7 s; sparks are rare pin-points that rise fast and die in under a second. Flakes only leave when scrolling forward. 5. **Time.** Scroll progress through the runway maps to t (the fire starts 5% in, slows toward the end, and goes out between 84% and 96%). t follows the scroll with a 0.12 s ease. A `heat` value goes to 1 while you scroll and decays over a few seconds when you stop: the ember brightness, its flicker and the noise clock all follow it, so the embers breathe on for a few seconds and then settle, dim and frozen, and the loop stops. Nothing burns per frame: the sheet is a pure function of t, so scrolling back unburns it exactly. ## Tuning - **Bands** are in `bands()`: scorch and ember widths in px (scaled to the sheet), char, ash and lift jitter as fractions of the whole burn. - **The front's shape**: the weights `0.42 big, 0.3 mid, 0.34 fibre` in the worker's speed (more contrast = more fingers), the blots, the edge boost (`0.45`), the fibre anisotropy (`0.5`). - **Embers**: `core`, `bead` thresholds and `wid` in the ember block of the shader; `ramp()` is the colour of temperature. - **Smoke, flakes, sparks**: spawn rates in `frame()`, looks in `PART_FS`. ## Theming | variable | default | used for | |---|---|---| | `--pb-sheet` | `#f7f0df` | the sheet (the shader adds fibres, laid and chain lines, toned edges, foxing and two fold creases) | | `--pb-ink` | `#2a1d14` | the ink | | `--pb-hand` | Homemade Apple | the face for the plain letter (and the canvas, which copies the `.pb-letter`'s font) | | `--pb-runway` | `460svh` | length of the scroll runway | | `--gutter` | | side padding of the plain letter | The page itself shows through the holes, so the piece takes whatever paper it sits on. ## Accessibility and motion - The letter is real text in the DOM: read aloud, found by ctrl+F, printed. Once the canvas is live it is visually hidden; the canvas is `aria-hidden` and never takes input (`pointer-events: none`). - Without JS or WebGL2 it is the plain letter on an ivory sheet. - Reduced motion: no runway; one still frame of the letter with its corner burned and the edge glowing (`data-rest`), no particles, no loop. - The stage is `touch-action: pan-y`; nothing captures a swipe. ## Cost - Precompute once per layout in a Worker: the Dijkstra over ~150k cells at 1440x900, run once or twice (~0.3-0.6 s), the ink canvas, and three small textures. Until it is ready the plain letter shows; on a resize the old frame stays up. - A frame is one fragment pass over the sheet (plus a 14px shadow margin): about 25 texture reads per burned pixel (Voronoi 3x3 twice, the field at five points, the shadow at four, the buckling at four), far fewer on fresh paper, then up to 420 point sprites. Drawn only while the scroll moves, for the few seconds of afterglow, or while particles are in the air, and only while the piece is on screen and the tab visible. Canvas DPR capped at 2. - Textures: burn time (R32F, fetched exactly and interpolated by hand), the same with speed and the blurred field (RGBA16F, filtered), the ink (RGBA8 at device size), the plates (RGBA8), noise (256²). ## Credits - [pretext](https://github.com/chenglou/pretext) by Cheng Lou, MIT (`vendor/pretext`, unmodified, see its `LICENSE` and `VERSION`). - Homemade Apple by Font Diner, via Google Fonts (Apache 2.0), loaded by the demo. - No images: the paper, the fire and the ash are drawn in the shader. `assets/credits.json` is empty. - The letter and the paragraphs around it were written for this component.
